newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia investment marred by political infighting.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia investment marred by political infighting.

text.p: The world of Cambodian business, already resembling a "Wild West" of the East, has grown more rough-and-tumble with increasing government infighting, business analysts said at the weekend.
As joint premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen vie for power ahead of next year's elections, an increasing number of investors fear being caught in the middle, they said.

"The word is out -- nothing major can be attempted until after the 1998 elections," said one diplomat. "Even small and medium-sized investors have to take care that they keep officials from both sides satisfied. If you only have one party behind a deal, it becomes inoperative."
The political fears compound concerns over an incomplete commercial code, corruption and war-scarred infrastructure.
Cambodia has no modern laws on contracts, trademarks, commercial arbitration, product liability or bankruptcy.
After decades of civil war, infrastructure is woefully inadequate, with poor and sometimes impassable roads, lack of power and an oversubscribed phone system.
Worse, say business people, security has not yet been completely restored. Corruption at all levels of government is a problem, and many businessmen use an entourage of bodyguards.
Three Taiwan businessmen were robbed early this year in separate incidents.
Particularly vulnerable to political infighting were investors in joint ventures with the government, analysts said.
If they were seen as aligned too strongly with one side -- Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC or Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) -- they could face attack from the other party.
Ranariddh recently declared null and void several agreements between Malaysia's Ariston Sdn Bhd and the government that were signed by a rival politician.
Ranariddh said proper legal procedures had not been followed and suggested leases for a golf course and resort and an airport concession agreement had taken on political overtones.
Ranariddh pointed out the agreements had been signed only by co-Minister of the Council of Ministers Sok An, of the CPP.
Analysts said at its best, Ranariddh's concern could reflect a desire that contracts are properly processed, or at worst, it could be interpreted as political partisanship.
The embattled national airline, Royal Air Cambodge, a joint venture between the government and Malaysia Helicopter Services, is widely viewed as a FUNCINPEC deal, incurring the wrath of CPP.
Hun Sen has publicly blamed the airline for "poor quality" and urged an open skies policy to end the carrier's monopoly on the domestic service.
The co-premiers formed an uneasy alliance following 1993 elections but will oppose each other next year.
Iain Gray, chief executive officer of the Malaysian firm Dragon Gold, which is developing a cargo hub at an unused airport in Cambodia, said he finalised his deal carefully.
"We have steered the whole thing, and we have spent equal time with FUNCINPEC and the CPP," he said.

Some small- and medium-sized businesses have enjoyed fewer problems, partly because of their low profile, noted Muh Tarng Shieh, director of the economic division of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in Phnom Penh.
He said Cambodia still had a cheap labour pool, little regulation and attractive investment incentives, and instability means land still comes cheap.
"Crisis means opportunity," he said in an interview.
